nodes.desc: Chinese Daoist philosopher of the Warring States period and author of the Zhuangzi. He champions spontaneous freedom, relativism and a simple natural life, refuses public office and scorns conventional morality and the ambitions of the state.

nodes.name: Laozi
nodes.desc: Chinese sage traditionally credited with the Dao De Jing and the founding of Daoism. He advocates wu wei, a ruler who barely governs, small peaceful states, a simple life and distrust of learning, weapons and luxury.

nodes.name: Mozi
nodes.desc: Chinese philosopher and founder of Mohism who preaches impartial care for all, rulers chosen by merit, frugality and only defensive war, and sees the will of Heaven as the basis of morality and politics.

nodes.name: Spartacus
nodes.desc: Thracian gladiator who led the largest slave revolt against Rome (73–71 BC). He raised an army of tens of thousands of enslaved people, defeated Roman legions and shared the plunder equally until Crassus crushed it.

nodes.name: Tiberius Gracchus
nodes.desc: Roman tribune of the plebs who proposed the 133 BC agrarian law, capping the public land held by the rich and giving it to the poor. He bypassed the Senate, appealed to the popular assembly and was killed by senators.

nodes.name: Gaius Gracchus
nodes.desc: Roman tribune of the plebs and brother of Tiberius, he passed subsidized grain sales, colonies, public works and court reform and proposed citizenship for the Latins. Hunted by the Senate, he died in 121 BC.

nodes.name: Mazdak
nodes.desc: Persian reformer of the Sasanian era who preached sharing of goods, an end to concentrated wealth and nonviolence. Backed by King Kavad I, he opened granaries in a famine but was massacred with his followers around 524.

nodes.name: John Ball
nodes.desc: English priest who preached equality ("When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?") and an end to serfdom, nobility and the church hierarchy. He was the voice of the 1381 Peasants' Revolt and was executed.

nodes.name: Wat Tyler
nodes.desc: Leader of the English Peasants' Revolt of 1381. He demanded an end to serfdom, low rents, free trade and the seizure of church property, always loyal to King Richard II; he was killed by an official at Smithfield.

nodes.name: Gerrard Winstanley
nodes.desc: 17th-century Englishman, leader of the Diggers and author of The Law of Freedom, who defended common land, an end to private land and wage labor, a republic and nonviolence, in a Christian and rationalist key.

nodes.name: Jean Meslier
nodes.desc: French priest who secretly wrote an atheist and communist Testament, attacking religion, monarchy, nobility and property and defending egalitarian parish communes. It was published only after his death.

nodes.name: Étienne de La Boétie
nodes.desc: French magistrate and humanist, author of the Discourse on Voluntary Servitude, which argues that tyranny survives only because people consent to it. He proposes peaceful refusal to obey, not violence, as the path to freedom.

nodes.name: William Godwin
nodes.desc: English philosopher and author of Political Justice, regarded as the father of philosophical anarchism. He defends abolishing government and unequal property, reason as the guide, education and nonviolence, and also criticizes marriage.

nodes.name: Thomas Spence
nodes.desc: English reformer who proposed that land belong to parishes, with rents paid into local funds financing services and an income for all. Jailed repeatedly for his radical pamphlets, he defended democracy.

nodes.name: Nestor Makhno
nodes.desc: Ukrainian anarchist who led the Revolutionary Insurgent Army of Ukraine (1918–1921) against Germans, Whites and Reds. He defended free communes, soviets and peasant self-management in the Free Territory until the Bolsheviks crushed it; he died in exile in Paris.

nodes.name: Élisée Reclus
nodes.desc: French geographer and anarchist, a Communard and author of the Universal Geography and Man and the Earth. He defends anarcho-communism, abolishing the state and property, vegetarianism, equality among peoples and harmony with nature.

nodes.name: Gary Johnson
nodes.desc: Former Republican governor of New Mexico (1995–2003) and Libertarian presidential candidate in 2012 and 2016. He defends cutting spending and taxes, legalizing marijuana, a balanced budget, free trade, more open immigration and less military intervention.

nodes.name: Chase Oliver
nodes.desc: Politician and 2024 Libertarian Party presidential candidate. He defends legalizing drugs, closing overseas bases, leaving NATO, ending military aid to Israel and Ukraine, open immigration reform, abortion rights, lower taxes and civil liberties.

nodes.name: João Amoêdo
nodes.desc: Banker, founder of the Novo Party and 2018 presidential candidate in Brazil. Economically liberal and socially conservative, he defends privatizing Petrobras and public banks, a leaner state and pension reform, and favors gun ownership while opposing drugs and abortion.

nodes.name: Jackson Hinkle
nodes.desc: American commentator and co-founder of the American Communist Party (2024). A self-described Marxist-Leninist who calls himself a Christian patriot, he defends Palestine, Putin's Russia and an end to US intervention abroad, and has been linked to the label "MAGA communism".

nodes.name: Zakhar Prilepin
nodes.desc: Russian writer and politician, former leader of the For Truth party and co-chair of A Just Russia until 2025. A left-wing nationalist with National Bolshevik roots, he backs Putin and the war in Ukraine, fought in the Donbas and defends a strong, social and imperial state.

nodes.name: Jordan Bardella
nodes.desc: President of the National Rally since 2022 and an MEP. He defends cutting immigration, national preference in benefits, law and order, sovereignty against the EU and tax cuts on energy, but backs sending weapons to Ukraine.

nodes.name: Santiago Abascal
nodes.desc: President of Vox since 2014 and a deputy for Madrid. He defends Spain's unity and an end to the autonomous regions, remigration and deportations, national priority, the traditional family, and opposes abortion, gender and climate agendas and high taxes.

nodes.name: Gatis Lagzdiņš (Sv3rige)
nodes.desc: Latvian YouTuber who advocates eating raw meat, flat Earth theory and opposition to veganism, with protests at vegan festivals, such as the 2019 London one that got him fined.

nodes.name: Aajonus Vonderplanitz
nodes.desc: American alternative nutritionist who advocated the Primal Diet of raw meat, eggs and dairy and founded Right to Choose Healthy Food for the right to raw milk, opposing the FDA, vaccines and conventional medicine.

nodes.name: Raphael Machado
nodes.desc: A lawyer trained at UFRJ and founder of Nova Resistência (2015), he spreads Dugin's Fourth Political Theory in Brazil: multipolarity, anti-Americanism, Vargas-style labor politics and Ibero-American integration.

nodes.name: Mark Rutte
nodes.desc: NATO Secretary General since 2024 and prime minister of the Netherlands for 14 years (2010–2024), leader of the VVD. A liberal conservative, he defends free markets, fiscal discipline, tighter asylum, support for Ukraine and 5% of GDP on defense.

nodes.name: Johannes Kaiser
nodes.desc: Chilean politician, activist and YouTuber, a deputy from 2022 to 2026 and founder of the National Libertarian Party. A paleolibertarian and reactionary, he defends a minimal state, free markets, hard immigration control, traditional values and Pinochet's legacy.

nodes.name: Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan
nodes.desc: Emir of Abu Dhabi (1966–2004) and first president of the United Arab Emirates, which he unified in 1971. An absolute, paternalistic monarch, he redistributed oil wealth, favoured mediation and foreign aid, and kept Islam as the basis of the state.

nodes.name: Carlos Drummond de Andrade
nodes.desc: Poet and chief of staff to the education minister under Vargas's authoritarian Estado Novo, later a newspaper columnist. A left-wing humanist, he wrote for a communist daily and published A Rosa do Povo (1945), poetry against war and oppression.

nodes.name: Graciliano Ramos
nodes.desc: Novelist and former small-town mayor, jailed without trial by the Vargas regime in 1936, which inspired Memórias do Cárcere. An atheist, he joined the Brazilian Communist Party in 1945 and portrayed the misery of the northeastern backlands in Barren Lives.

nodes.name: Euclides da Cunha
nodes.desc: Military engineer, republican and positivist, he covered the Canudos War for a São Paulo newspaper and wrote Rebellion in the Backlands, which condemns the massacre of the rural settlers. He later denounced the exploitation of Amazon rubber tappers.

nodes.name: Necmettin Erbakan
nodes.desc: Turkish engineer and professor, founder of the Islamist Milli Görüş movement and prime minister (1996–97) until the military forced him out. He advocated an interest-free Just Order, domestic heavy industry and economic integration of Muslim countries (D-8).

nodes.name: Péter Magyar
nodes.desc: Lawyer and former Fidesz insider who broke with Orbán in 2024 and led Tisza to victory in 2026, becoming Hungary's prime minister. He promises rule of law, anti-corruption and alignment with the EU and NATO, while keeping a hard line on migration.

nodes.name: Suharto
nodes.desc: Indonesian general who ruled the so-called New Order from 1967 to 1998, with the army at the center of the state, an official party (Golkar), anticommunism (the 1965–66 massacres), liberal technocrats and rapid growth, but also corruption and repression.

nodes.name: Hayato Ikeda
nodes.desc: Japanese prime minister from 1960 to 1964, a former Finance Ministry bureaucrat who replaced the debate over the US treaty with the Income Doubling Plan and led Japan to the peak of its economic miracle and the Tokyo Olympics.

nodes.name: Shigeru Yoshida
nodes.desc: Japanese diplomat and prime minister (1946–47, 1948–54) who rebuilt the country under the American occupation, accepted the pacifist Constitution, signed the San Francisco Treaty and set the Yoshida Doctrine: security with the US, effort on the economy.

nodes.name: Oscar Niemeyer
nodes.desc: Brazilian architect who designed the buildings of Brasília at Kubitschek's invitation and took curved modernism to the world, always a Communist Party militant and critic of inequality, which cost him exile under the dictatorship.

nodes.name: Chiang Ching-kuo
nodes.desc: Son of Chiang Kai-shek, trained in the Soviet Union, he headed the Kuomintang's political police, served as premier and president of Taiwan (1978–88), carried out the Ten Major Construction Projects and, late in life, lifted martial law and opened the democratic transition.

nodes.name: Raúl Prebisch
nodes.desc: An Argentine economist, Prebisch created the center–periphery thesis and led ECLAC and UNCTAD, advocating industrialization and regional integration so Latin America could escape deteriorating terms of trade.

nodes.name: Michał Kalecki
nodes.desc: A Polish Marxist economist, Kalecki anticipated Keynes's theory of effective demand, analyzed the political business cycle of full employment, and worked in socialist Poland's planning while protesting the antisemitic purge of 1968.

nodes.name: Dmitry Medvedev
nodes.desc: President of Russia (2008–2012) and Putin's prime minister, Medvedev, who pitched himself as a technological modernizer, turned hawk: deputy chairman of the Security Council, he threatens nuclear weapons and defends the war in Ukraine.

nodes.name: Giovanni Gentile
nodes.desc: An idealist philosopher of actualism, Gentile was Mussolini's education minister, reformed Italian schooling, wrote the Manifesto of Fascist Intellectuals and fascism's doctrinal core, and was killed by partisans in 1944.

nodes.name: Itamar Franco
nodes.desc: A politician from Minas Gerais, Itamar took the presidency after Collor's impeachment (1992–94), launched the Real Plan, defended a strong state in the economy and, as state governor, declared a moratorium on his state's debt to the federal government.

nodes.name: Fernando Collor
nodes.desc: Elected president (1990–92) as a "hunter of maharajas" against inflated public salaries, Collor froze savings accounts in his stabilization plan, opened the economy and began privatizations; he resigned facing impeachment and, as senator, was convicted of corruption in 2023.

nodes.name: Júlio Prestes
nodes.desc: A politician of São Paulo's Republican Party and governor of São Paulo (1927–30), Júlio Prestes won the 1930 presidential election under the coffee-and-milk oligarchic pact, but was barred from taking office by the 1930 Revolution.

nodes.name: João Figueiredo
nodes.desc: A general and the last president of the military dictatorship (1979–85), Figueiredo signed the Amnesty Law and led a controlled opening, but kept up repression, rejected the direct-elections campaign and faced the foreign debt crisis.

nodes.name: John Adams
nodes.desc: A founder and the second president of the United States, Adams led the Federalists, defended a mixed government with a strong executive and an elite Senate, avoided war with France and signed the Alien and Sedition Acts.

nodes.name: James Monroe
nodes.desc: The fifth president of the United States, Monroe presided over the Era of Good Feelings, proclaimed the Monroe Doctrine against European recolonization of the Americas, bought Florida and signed the Missouri Compromise, upholding slavery.

nodes.name: Allan Kardec
nodes.desc: A French educator, Kardec codified Spiritism in The Spirits' Book (1857): God, reincarnation and moral evolution, charity above dogma and no clergy, reconciling science and faith while staying out of party politics.

nodes.name: Bezerra de Menezes
nodes.desc: A physician and liberal politician of the Brazilian Empire, a city councillor and deputy known as the "Doctor of the Poor", he embraced Spiritism in 1886 and presided over the Brazilian Spiritist Federation, making charity and Kardec's doctrine its foundation in Brazil.

nodes.name: Miguel Primo de Rivera
nodes.desc: General and dictator of Spain from 1923 to 1930, Marquis of Estella: backed by Alfonso XIII, he suspended the Constitution, created the Patriotic Union and ruled through censorship, public works, corporatism and repression of Catalanism.

nodes.name: Elias Jabbour
nodes.desc: UERJ economist and geographer, PCdoB leader and author of China: Socialism of the 21st Century; he defends market socialism, a project-based economy with the state as chief entrepreneur, and a China-led multipolar world.

nodes.name: Ted Cruz
nodes.desc: Republican senator from Texas since 2013 and 2016 presidential candidate, a constitutional lawyer and evangelical Christian. He defends tax cuts, free trade, border control, firm support for Israel and a hard line on Iran and China.

nodes.name: Ben Sasse
nodes.desc: Historian and former Republican senator from Nebraska (2015–2023), later president of the University of Florida. A critic of Trump populism, he defends free markets, federalism, entitlement reform, support for Ukraine and a hard line on China and Russia.

nodes.name: Pete Hegseth
nodes.desc: Army veteran and former Fox News host, he has led the Pentagon (renamed Department of War) since 2025. He defends a warrior ethos, cuts to diversity programs, a ban on transgender troops, Christian nationalism and military action against cartels.

nodes.name: Rand Paul
nodes.desc: Ophthalmologist and Republican senator from Kentucky since 2011, son of Ron Paul. A conservative libertarian, he defends minimal government, spending cuts, ending the president's tariff power, non-intervention and limits on surveillance; opposes abortion.

nodes.name: Heinrich Himmler
nodes.desc: Reichsführer-SS, Himmler headed the SS, the Gestapo and the German police, organized the concentration and extermination camps and carried out the Holocaust, along with Germanization projects and racial mysticism. He killed himself on capture in 1945.

nodes.name: Alexander Rüstow
nodes.desc: German sociologist and economist, Rüstow popularized the term neoliberalism at the 1938 Walter Lippmann Colloquium and defended a vital liberalism: a strong state against monopolies, social policy and a critique of laissez-faire. He lived in exile in Turkey during Nazism.

nodes.name: Alfred Müller-Armack
nodes.desc: Economist and Erhard's state secretary, Müller-Armack coined the term social market economy in 1946 and shaped it as a synthesis of free markets and social policy, the basis of the German economic miracle. He also championed European integration.

nodes.name: Walter Eucken
nodes.desc: German economist of the Freiburg School and an opponent of Nazism, Eucken founded ordoliberalism: he defended a competitive order guaranteed by a strong state, against monopolies, cartels and central planning. He inspired the German social market economy.

nodes.name: John A. Macdonald
nodes.desc: Canada's first prime minister, a Conservative and architect of the 1867 Confederation: he built the transcontinental railway, adopted the protectionist National Policy tariffs, crushed the Métis Rebellion and created the Indigenous residential schools.

nodes.name: Pierre Poilievre
nodes.desc: Leader of the Conservative Party since 2022: he vows to cut taxes and the carbon tax, tie immigration to housing supply, toughen sentences, defund the CBC and back pipelines and bitcoin, in a populist message against the elites.

nodes.name: Benito Juárez
nodes.desc: Liberal president of Mexico (1858–1872) of Zapotec origin: he led the Reform, which separated church and state and seized clerical property, resisted the French intervention, had Maximilian shot and governed with emergency powers.

nodes.name: Porfirio Díaz
nodes.desc: Dictator-president of Mexico for about 30 years (1876–1911): he imposed "order and progress" through rural police and repression, drew in foreign capital, railways and large estates, made peace with the Church and fell to the Mexican Revolution.

nodes.name: Andrés Manuel López Obrador
nodes.desc: President of Mexico (2018–2024) for Morena: a left-wing nationalism that strengthened Pemex and CFE, expanded pensions and welfare programs, put public security in the Army's hands, attacked autonomous agencies and approved popular election of judges.

nodes.name: Robert Menzies
nodes.desc: Prime minister of Australia (1939–1941, 1949–1966) and founder of the Liberal Party: an Anglophile monarchist and anti-communist (he tried to ban the Communist Party), sent troops to Korea and Vietnam and kept the White Australia policy.

nodes.name: John Howard
nodes.desc: Conservative prime minister of Australia (1996–2007): he restricted guns after Port Arthur, introduced the GST, privatised Telstra, deregulated labour, hardened immigration and sent troops to Iraq and Afghanistan.

nodes.name: Roger Douglas
nodes.desc: New Zealand Finance Minister (1984–88) in the Lange Labour government, he devised Rogernomics: a floating dollar, privatisations, the end of subsidies and a consumption tax. He later co-founded the liberal ACT party.

nodes.name: Fethullah Gülen
nodes.desc: Turkish preacher and theologian, leader of the Hizmet movement: he promoted education, science, interfaith dialogue and Islam in public life, condemning the politicization of religion. Exiled in the US since 1999, he denied Ankara's charge of ordering the 2016 coup.

nodes.name: Osama bin Laden
nodes.desc: Saudi founder of al-Qaeda: he financed the anti-Soviet jihad in Afghanistan, declared war on the US in 1996 over its military presence in Saudi Arabia, and sought a caliphate under sharia. He planned the 9/11 attacks and was killed in Pakistan in 2011.

nodes.name: Jânio Quadros
nodes.desc: Governor of São Paulo, he won the presidency in 1961 on an anti-corruption "broom" platform, pursued an independent foreign policy and decorated Che Guevara. He resigned after seven months, opening the crisis that preceded the 1964 coup.

nodes.name: Ulysses Guimarães
nodes.desc: MDB president, he was the 1974 "anti-candidate" against the dictatorship, led the Diretas Já campaign and presided over the Constituent Assembly, promulgating the "Citizen Constitution" of 1988. He ran for president in 1989 and died in a helicopter crash in 1992.

nodes.name: Paulo Maluf
nodes.desc: Engineer and businessman, he was mayor and governor of São Paulo and a presidential candidate in 1985 and 1989. Tied to the quip "he steals but gets things done" and to major road works, he was convicted of money laundering and serves house arrest.

nodes.name: José Maria Eymael
nodes.desc: Lawyer from São Paulo and constituent assembly member, he founded the Democracia Cristã party. A six-time presidential candidate (1998 and 2006 to 2022), never above 1%, he is known for the "Ey, Ey, Eymael" jingle and for defending Catholic social teaching.

nodes.name: José Serra
nodes.desc: Economist, former student union president and exile under the dictatorship, he was health minister (generic drugs law), mayor and governor of São Paulo, senator and foreign minister. He lost the presidency in 2002 and 2010 and criticized high interest rates.

nodes.name: Anthony Garotinho
nodes.desc: Radio host and evangelical, he was mayor of Campos, governor of Rio de Janeiro (1999–2002), with welfare programs like Cheque Cidadão, and finished third in the 2002 presidential election. He was jailed in 2016 and 2017 on corruption and vote-buying charges.

nodes.name: Aécio Neves
nodes.desc: Grandson of Tancredo Neves, he presided over the lower house, governed Minas Gerais (2003–10) and was a senator. The PSDB's 2014 candidate, he lost to Dilma Rousseff by just over 3 points. Named in the 2017 JBS plea deal, he left the party leadership.

nodes.name: Cabo Daciolo
nodes.desc: Military firefighter and evangelical pastor, he was a federal deputy (2015–19), elected for PSOL, and the Patriota party's 2018 presidential candidate (6th place). He proposed writing "all power emanates from God" into the Constitution and denounces a "New World Order".

nodes.name: Henrique Meirelles
nodes.desc: Banker who led BankBoston and served as Central Bank president for eight years (2003–10) under Lula. As Temer's finance minister he pushed the spending cap and pension reform; the MDB's 2018 presidential candidate, he won 1.2% of the vote.

nodes.name: Felipe d'Avila
nodes.desc: Political scientist and founder of the Centro de Liderança Pública, he was the Novo party's 2022 presidential candidate, with under 1% of the vote. He defended a lean state, privatizations, administrative and tax reform, and economic freedom.

nodes.name: Rupert Lowe
nodes.desc: Elected as a Reform UK MP in 2024 and suspended in 2025, founded Restore Britain. Campaigns for net negative immigration, mass deportations, an end to asylum, a burqa ban, a lean state and for Britain to stay "a Christian country".

nodes.name: James Talarico
nodes.desc: Texas Democrat, state representative since 2018 and Presbyterian seminarian. He backs universal health care, legal abortion and church-state separation, yet calls himself tough on border security. Elected U.S. senator in 2026, defeating Ken Paxton.

nodes.name: Roy Cooper
nodes.desc: North Carolina Democrat, attorney general (2001–2017) and governor (2017–2025). He vetoed abortion restrictions and local-ICE-cooperation bills, expanded Medicaid and opposes Trump’s tariffs. Elected U.S. senator in 2026, defeating Michael Whatley.

nodes.name: Abdul El-Sayed
nodes.desc: Michigan Democratic physician who ran public health in Detroit (2015–2017) and Wayne County. He backs Medicare for All, abolishing ICE, ending military aid to Israel and public ownership of AI. Elected U.S. senator in 2026, defeating Mike Rogers.

nodes.name: Cleitinho Azevedo
nodes.desc: Senator for Minas Gerais since 2023 (Republicanos) and governor-elect in 2026, winning the first round with 55% of the vote. He backed amnesty for the January 8 rioters and privatizing state utilities, but in 2026 ruled out selling the power company Cemig.

nodes.name: Arnold Schwarzenegger
nodes.desc: Austrian-American actor and bodybuilder who served as Republican governor of California (2003–2011). He signed the AB 32 climate law and backed independent redistricting; in 2025 he criticized Trump and opposed Proposition 50.

nodes.name: Eduardo Campos
nodes.desc: Governor of Pernambuco (2007–2014) for the Brazilian Socialist Party and former science minister under Lula, he launched the Pact for Life homicide-reduction program. Running for president in 2014 with Marina Silva, he died in a plane crash in Santos that August.

nodes.name: Jorginho Mello
nodes.desc: Governor of Santa Catarina (Liberal Party) since 2023, re-elected in 2026, ally of Jair Bolsonaro and former senator. He signed laws banning racial quotas at state universities and letting parents opt out of gender-identity classes, and signaled selling the water utility.

nodes.name: Tancredo Neves
nodes.desc: Brazilian politician who served as President Vargas’s justice minister and as prime minister under a brief parliamentary system (1961–62). Governor of Minas Gerais, he led the opposition alliance and won the 1985 indirect presidential vote, but died before inauguration.

nodes.name: Chico Mendes
nodes.desc: Amazonian rubber tapper, union leader and Workers’ Party co-founder in Acre. He led peaceful standoffs against deforestation, helped found the National Council of Rubber Tappers (1985) and championed extractive reserves. Ranchers murdered him in 1988.

nodes.name: Miguel Arraes
nodes.desc: Three-time governor of Pernambuco. In 1963 he brokered a wage pact between sugar-mill owners and cane workers, was ousted and jailed in the 1964 coup, lived in exile in Algeria until 1979 and later led the Brazilian Socialist Party.

nodes.name: Rafael Fonteles
nodes.desc: Mathematician and Workers’ Party politician, governor of Piauí since 2023 and its finance secretary in 2015–2022. He granted water and sewage services to a private operator in 2024, set a spending cap and was re-elected in 2026 with over 70% of the vote.

nodes.name: Luís Montenegro
nodes.desc: Lawyer and PSD leader, prime minister of Portugal since 2024. Re-elected in the 2025 snap election, he passed tougher foreigners and nationality laws with Chega’s votes and is partially privatizing TAP.

nodes.name: Rob Jetten
nodes.desc: Leader of the centrist-liberal D66 and Prime Minister of the Netherlands since February 2026, heading a minority coalition with the VVD and CDA. Former climate minister (2022–24), he backs new nuclear plants and defence spending of 3.5% of GDP.

nodes.name: Andrej Babiš
nodes.desc: Billionaire owner of Agrofert and founder of ANO 2011, he was Czech prime minister in 2017–21 and returned in December 2025 with the SPD and Motorists. His government rejects the EU Migration Pact and ETS2; the Čapí hnízdo fraud case is stalled by immunity.

nodes.name: Robert Fico
nodes.desc: Slovak prime minister for a third time since 2023 and leader of Smer-SD. He survived a 2024 shooting, ended state military aid to Ukraine, attended Moscow’s 2025 Victory Day parade and passed a two-sexes constitutional amendment.

nodes.name: Alexander Stubb
nodes.desc: Finland’s president since 2024 and former prime minister (2014–15) for the National Coalition. He backs NATO and Ukraine, practises “values-based realism”, keeps a dialogue with Trump, and has floated an EU of up to 40 countries.

nodes.name: Sébastien Lecornu
nodes.desc: French politician, prime minister since 2025 and former Armed Forces minister. He steered the 2024–2030 military programming law and, in office, suspended the pension reform and governed without a majority, using Article 49.3 for the 2026 budget.

nodes.name: John Healey
nodes.desc: British Labour politician. Served as Defence Secretary (2024–2026) and resigned over what he called inadequate military funding. Became Chancellor of the Exchequer in July 2026 under Andy Burnham.

nodes.name: Édouard Philippe
nodes.desc: Former prime minister of France (2017–2020) under Macron, mayor of Le Havre and founder of Horizons. Declared a 2027 presidential bid in 2024 and in 2025 urged Macron to leave office early.

nodes.name: Klemens von Metternich
nodes.desc: Austrian diplomat, foreign minister from 1809 to 1848 and state chancellor from 1821. A chief architect of the Congress of Vienna, he led Europe’s conservative order and the Carlsbad Decrees until the 1848 revolution forced him out.

nodes.name: Jean Monnet
nodes.desc: French cognac merchant, never elected, who led France’s postwar modernization plan (1946), drafted the Schuman Declaration (1950) and presided over the ECSC High Authority (1952–1955). A founding father of Europe.

nodes.name: Mario Draghi
nodes.desc: Italian economist who led the European Central Bank (2011–2019), pledging in 2012 to do “whatever it takes” for the euro. Prime Minister of Italy 2021–2022; behind the 2024 Draghi Report on EU competitiveness.

nodes.name: António Costa
nodes.desc: Portuguese Socialist, prime minister 2015–2023: governed with the Left Bloc and Communists, ran a budget surplus and resigned after Operation Influencer. Since December 2024 he has chaired the European Council.

nodes.name: André Ventura
nodes.desc: Founder and leader of Chega, a Portuguese national-populist party. Backs immigration quotas, life imprisonment and constitutional revision. Lost the 2026 presidential runoff to António José Seguro with 33%.

nodes.name: Mário Soares
nodes.desc: Founder of the Socialist Party, jailed and exiled under the Estado Novo. He faced down the Communists in 1975, as prime minister took Portugal into the EEC (1985), and was president from 1986 to 1996.

nodes.name: Álvaro Cunhal
nodes.desc: General secretary of the Portuguese Communist Party (1961–1992), jailed by the Estado Novo, he escaped Peniche in 1960. A central figure of the 1974–75 revolution, he backed land reform, nationalizations and the USSR.

nodes.name: Clement Attlee
nodes.desc: Labour leader and British prime minister (1945–51). His government created the NHS, nationalised coal, railways and the Bank of England, granted India independence and took Britain into NATO.

nodes.name: David Cameron
nodes.desc: British Conservative, prime minister from 2010 to 2016. Led a coalition, legalised same-sex marriage, imposed austerity, called the Brexit referendum, lost it and resigned. Served as Foreign Secretary in 2023–24.

nodes.name: Felipe González
nodes.desc: Spanish Socialist leader (PSOE, 1974–1997) and four-term prime minister (1982–1996). He dropped Marxism, took Spain into the EEC and kept it in NATO; the GAL dirty war and corruption scandals marked his exit.

nodes.name: José María Aznar
nodes.desc: Prime Minister of Spain (1996–2004) for the People’s Party. Privatized Telefónica and Repsol, took Spain into the euro, hardened policy against ETA and backed the Iraq invasion. Chairs FAES, a conservative-liberal think tank.

nodes.name: José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero
nodes.desc: PSOE leader and Spain’s prime minister (2004–2011): he withdrew troops from Iraq, legalized same-sex marriage and met the crisis with austerity. A Venezuela mediator, he is under investigation in the Plus Ultra case.

nodes.name: Mariano Rajoy
nodes.desc: Popular Party politician who governed Spain from 2011 to 2018: absolute majority, bank bailout and fiscal austerity. He faced the Catalan referendum and party corruption, and fell to a no-confidence motion.

nodes.name: Adolfo Suárez
nodes.desc: Former Francoist Movement minister who served as Spain’s prime minister (1976–1981) during the Transition: he steered the Political Reform Law, legalized the Communist Party, signed the Moncloa Pacts and stayed seated during the 1981 coup attempt.

nodes.name: Mauricio Macri
nodes.desc: Argentine businessman and politician. Led Boca Juniors, governed Buenos Aires and served as president (2015–2019), freeing the peso and borrowing from the IMF. Founded the PRO and leads it today.

nodes.name: Raúl Alfonsín
nodes.desc: Argentine UCR president (1983–1989) who restored democracy after the dictatorship: created the CONADEP and tried the Juntas, but yielded with Punto Final and Obediencia Debida; the Austral Plan failed to stop hyperinflation.

nodes.name: Alberto Fernández
nodes.desc: Peronist lawyer, cabinet chief under Néstor Kirchner and president of Argentina (2019–2023). He renegotiated the debt and the IMF deal, imposed the pandemic lockdown and signed legal abortion into law; he faces ongoing court proceedings.

nodes.name: Jorge Rafael Videla
nodes.desc: Army general who led the 1976 coup and headed the military junta until 1981. His regime practised state terrorism, with thousands of disappeared. Sentenced to life in 1985 and again in 2010, he died in prison in 2013.

nodes.name: Willy Brandt
nodes.desc: German Social Democrat, exiled under the Nazis and mayor of West Berlin. As chancellor he launched Ostpolitik, with treaties with Moscow and Warsaw, and knelt at the Warsaw Ghetto. Nobel Peace Prize in 1971; resigned after the Guillaume affair.

nodes.name: Nicolas Sarkozy
nodes.desc: Right-wing politician, mayor of Neuilly, interior minister and president of France (2007–2012). He raised the retirement age, brought France back into NATO’s military command and led the Libya intervention. He has two final convictions and one at first instance.

nodes.name: Goh Keng Swee
nodes.desc: Economist and deputy prime minister of Singapore under Lee Kuan Yew. He created the Economic Development Board and the Jurong industrial estate, drew in multinationals, and built the national service system and the armed forces.

nodes.name: Delfim Netto
nodes.desc: Economist and finance minister (1967–1974), later agriculture and planning minister, under Brazil's military dictatorship. He ran the "economic miracle" and signed Institutional Act No. 5. He was a congressman for about 20 years and an informal adviser to Lula.

nodes.name: Sergei Korolev
nodes.desc: Soviet rocket engineer, chief designer of the R-7 rocket, Sputnik and Gagarin's flight. Arrested in 1938 in the Great Purge and sent to Kolyma, he later worked in a sharashka prison lab; his name stayed secret until his death.

nodes.name: Zhou Enlai
nodes.desc: Revolutionary and diplomat, premier of China from 1949 to 1976 and Mao's right hand. He led the diplomacy of Bandung and the 1972 opening to the US, proposed the Four Modernizations and shielded some officials during the Cultural Revolution.

nodes.name: Zhu Rongji
nodes.desc: Mayor of Shanghai and premier of China from 1998 to 2003. He restructured state firms with mass layoffs, cleaned up the banks, tamed inflation and negotiated China's 2001 entry into the WTO. He was purged as a "rightist" in 1958.

nodes.name: Paul Volcker
nodes.desc: Chairman of the Federal Reserve from 1979 to 1987, appointed by Carter and kept by Reagan. He pushed interest rates near 20% to break inflation, causing a deep recession. He later proposed the Volcker Rule, which limits bank speculation.

nodes.name: Domingo Cavallo
nodes.desc: Argentine economist, foreign minister and economy minister under Menem and later De la Rúa. He created Convertibility, which pegged the peso to the dollar and ended hyperinflation; the 2001 "corralito" preceded the crisis and the government's fall.

nodes.name: Michael Jackson
nodes.desc: American singer and dancer, creator of Thriller. He paired fame with philanthropy in "We Are the World" and "Heal the World" (the Heal the World Foundation), sang against racism and war, and criticized the music industry; child abuse allegations marked his life.

nodes.name: Charlie Chaplin
nodes.desc: British actor and filmmaker, creator of The Tramp. He satirized industrialization in Modern Times and Nazism in The Great Dictator. Accused of communist sympathies during McCarthyism, he was barred from re-entering the US in 1952.

nodes.name: Bob Dylan
nodes.desc: American singer-songwriter, the voice of 1960s folk. "Blowin' in the Wind" and "The Times They Are a-Changin'" became civil rights anthems; he later rejected the spokesman role. He had a born-again Christian phase (1979–81) and won the Nobel in 2016.

nodes.name: John Lennon
nodes.desc: British musician, co-founder of the Beatles. As a solo artist he sang "Imagine" and "Give Peace a Chance", campaigned against the Vietnam War with Yoko Ono and was surveilled by Nixon's FBI. He was murdered in New York in 1980.

nodes.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
nodes.desc: German composer, bridge between Classicism and Romanticism. He admired Enlightenment and republican ideals, struck out the dedication to Napoleon when he became emperor, and set Schiller's "Ode to Joy", on human brotherhood, in the Ninth Symphony.

nodes.name: Víctor Jara
nodes.desc: Chilean singer, theater director and communist activist, a leading figure of the Nueva Canción Chilena. He backed Allende's Popular Unity with songs like "Te recuerdo, Amanda". He was arrested, tortured and killed by Pinochet's regime at Chile Stadium in 1973.

nodes.name: Muhammad Ali
nodes.desc: American boxer, three-time heavyweight champion. He converted to Islam through the Nation of Islam and refused Vietnam draft induction as a conscientious objector, losing his title and license for years; he became a civil rights symbol and later a peace ambassador.

nodes.name: Diego Maradona
nodes.desc: Argentine footballer, captain of the 1986 World Cup winners and an idol in Naples. He declared himself on the left, admired Fidel Castro, Chávez and Che Guevara, criticized the US and the IMF, and backed the Kirchner governments and Maduro.

nodes.name: Sócrates
nodes.desc: Doctor and Brazil national team midfielder, Corinthians captain. He led the Democracia Corinthiana (1982–84), in which players voted on club decisions, and backed the Diretas Já campaign and the Workers' Party (PT); he wrote as a political columnist.

nodes.name: George Weah
nodes.desc: Liberian former striker, 1995 Ballon d'Or and World Player of the Year. He was president of Liberia from 2018 to 2024, running a centre-left populist program on poverty and infrastructure, amid corruption criticism; he lost reelection to Boakai and leads the CDC.

nodes.name: Pedro Alliana
nodes.desc: Colorado Party politician and vice president of Paraguay since 2023. He was governor of Ñeembucú, deputy, Chamber president and party president (until 2023). A Horacio Cartes ally, he is the 2028 presidential hopeful and tipped to succeed Peña.
